If you want to get into cycling and don't know what type of bike to buy, this post might be helpful as a primer. It doesn't cover all variations of bicycle (they are innumerable), and there are even variations within variations within variations, but this will give you a basic outline of 3 of the most popular categories of bike to choose from.

#**Comfort bike**

Upright seating position, wide tires, smaller wheels (26"), smaller chain rings, triple crankset, flat handlebars, front shocks, and a suspension seatpost. These bikes are designed with comfort in mind over all other considerations.

Because the handlebars go above the saddle, the rider is put in a very natural upright non-aerodynamic posture, maximizing his or her comfort and ability to pay attention to the scenery. Saddles on these bikes are usually wide, short in length, and heavily padded. A spring built into the seatpost keeps road bumps from traveling up the bike and slamming the rider in the butt. The wider tires also help dampen vibration, but increase the rolling resistance of the bike. The smaller front chain rings make pedaling easier, but makes the rider tend to be slower overall. The front shocks also make the ride smoother at the cost of riding efficiency. The 26" rims are stronger and better suited for heavier riders.

Overall, these bikes are slow but comfortable and enjoyable to ride, especially for beginners. They can be used for road riding and light trail riding. Because of the triple crankset (3 front chain rings) and easier gear combinations, comfort bikes can be pretty decent for hill climbing and carrying cargo.

#**Hybrid Bike**

Forward leaning seating position, adjustable stem, standard wheel size for a road bike (700c), medium to small tire width, normal size chain rings, triple crankset, flat handlebars, rigid frame. These are great recreational or commuter bikes that can be used to ride relatively fast and tackle variable terrain.

Somewhere between a mountain bike and a road bike, these have flat handlebars that are low, putting the rider in a more forward leaning aerodynamic position, and often have an adjustable stem to allow the rider to move the handlebars higher or lower as they like. The medium to small tire width allows for less rolling resistance while leaving room for some vibration dampening, and the larger road bike sized 700c rims are good for maintaining speed over longer distances. The frame is rigid and lacks shocks, increasing rider efficiency by maximizing power transfer to forward momentum. The triple crankset gives you a wide range of gears for hill climbing or picking up speed on descents and flat ground.

These type of bikes are very respectable and popular, and with good reason. They are great recreational or commuter bikes that can handle the odd rough patch of road and have enough gearing to conquer basically anything a city or suburb could throw your way.

#**Road bike**

Aggressive riding position, rigid frame, narrow tires, large rims (700c), curved drop style handlebars, double crankset. A road bike is a performance machine built for speed at the sacrifice of comfort.

The most distinctive feature of a road bike is probably the curved drop bars. Road bike handlebars are already low, forcing the rider into a downward leaning position to minimize wind resistance, but the drop bars allow the rider to get even lower. The bars afford the rider several different riding positions. They can ride with hands on the top of the bars, or extend their hands to grip around the top of the brake hoods where they may use the brakes or shifters, or they can lower their hands to rest at the bottom end of the drops, or push forward to the inside curve of the drops where the brakes and shifters may also be reached. A 3rd braking position may be added by installing inline brake levers, but this is not common for a road bike.

Road bikes are meant to be stiff and lightweight, with gearing meant for speed. For an inexperienced rider, a road bike can be a torture device. Their narrow hard saddles can take some getting used to, and the aggressively forward leading posture one is forced into can be strenuous and painful if one hasn't developed the proper muscle control and endurance for it. Their skinny tires are great for reducing rolling resistance, but don't offer much vibration dampening. This can greatly reduce the smoothness of the ride depending on road conditions, especially when combined with the deliberate stiffness of the frame.

People often wrongly assume that road bikes are "fast". Road bikes are not fast. Road bikes merely allow a fast rider to more optimally make use of their ability to output raw power toward the goal of being fast. No bike is "fast". Riders are (or are not) fast. The rider is the engine, and a bad engine on a good bike is still going to be slower than a good engine on a bad bike.

----------

I hope this was helpful. I might cover more types of bikes if there is a positive enough response. There are so many! There's also so much to cover about each different type of bike... sadly far too much for a short overview like this.
